LV wall thickness should be performed at end-diastole, preferably in short-axis views and all LV
segments from base to apex should be examined with the wall thickness recorded at the mitral, mid-
LV, and apical levels. In an adult, HCM is defined by a wall thickness ≥15 mm in one or more LV
myocardial segments [57]. However, elite athletes participating in sports with high static and mixed
sports can display profound LV remodeling that can be confused with HCM [38, 56]. Nevertheless, the
presence of systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve against the interventricular system with a LV
outflow tract (LVOT) pressure gradient is inconsistent with a diagnosis of athlete‘s heart and strongly
suggests HCM in the athlete [55,57].

   The LV outflow tract obstruction in HCM is caused by asymmetrical septal hypertrophy, an
fibrofatty myocardial involvement, and history of high intensity or endurance exercise routine. An
international collaboration has derived a risk calculator for the prediction of sustained ventricular
dysrhythmias, ventricular fibrillation or cardiac arrest/sudden cardiac death in individuals with definite
ACM [96, 97]. On the basis of components of age at diagnosis, sex, cardiac syncope, extent of ECG T
wave inversion, 24-hour premature ventricular complex count, history of non-sustained ventricular
tachycardia, and the RV ejection fraction, a 5-year risk score can be obtained. The calculator of the
ACM risk score is available at http://ACMrisk.com [96, 97, 98].

TREATMENT

Restriction of exercise activity is extremely important in the management of individuals with ACM
because restriction of exercise intensity and duration significantly decreases the amount of ventricular
dysrhythmias. Athletes with ACM should be restricted to low level activity such as 30 minutes of brisk
walking per day, because exercise levels >650 MET-hours per year accelerate the phenotypic
expression of ACM [99-101]. Exercise restriction should also be advised in athletes and in family
members who are genotype positive but phenotype negative in order to delay potential phenotypic
expression and should also be considered in athletes with borderline or possible ACM [91,102, 103].

  The use of beta-adrenergic receptor antagonists is recommended in athletes with ACM and non-
sustained ventricular tachycardia or other ventricular dysrhythmias [91]. Adjuvant pharmacotherapy
with flecainide or amiodarone should be considered in athletes with ongoing ventricular dysrhythmias
despite the use of a beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist [104]. However, therapy with beta adrenergic
receptor antagonists, flecainide, amiodarone or ventricular ablation of endocardial/epicardial
ventricular tachycardia foci does not obviate the need for ICDs in high risk athletes as determined by
the ACM risk score [91, 99, 105, 106]. For athletes with asymptomatic but significant RV and/or LV
 reduction in ejection fractions, treatment with angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin
II receptor blockers should also be considered [99].

  The decision to insert an ICD in an athlete for primary preventions requires thorough evaluation of
the risk of sudden cardiac death and the risk of ICD device-related complications, which include a 3.9%
annual rate of shocks and a 4.2% annual rate of complications such as infection or lead malfunction
[107]... In those athletes with a 5% to 15% 5-year risk with a history of aborted cardiac arrest or sudden
cardiac death, sustain ventricular tachycardia, severe RV, LV or biventricular dysfunction, an ICD is
indicated [99, 108, 109]. In those athletes with intermediate risk with >1 major risk factor such as
syncope, non-sustain ventricular tachycardia, moderate ventricular dysfunction, an ICD should be
considered. In those athletes with >I minor risk factors, an ICD may be considered and in those
athletes with <5% 5-year risk, an ICD is not recommended [99, 108, 109]. For athletes undergoing ICD
implantation for primary prevention of ventricular dysrhythmias, a subcutaneous ICD should be
considered whereas for athletes who present with sustained monomorphic VT, an endocardial ICD
device should be considered because of the risk of recurrent sustained dysrhythmias. Finally, athletes
with uncontrollable ventricular tachydysrhythmias or intractable heart failure require evaluation for
heart transplantation [110].

Athletes with ACM require reevaluation every one to two years for new onset or worsening of
symptoms, progression of ventricular myocardial abnormalities, and supraventricular and ventricular
dysrhythmias. In these athletes, the risk of sudden cardiac arrest/death should be re-assessed and
treatment further optimized [99].



ATHLETES WITH IMPLANTABLE CARDIOVERTERS-DEFIBRILLATORS (ICDs)

In individuals of all ages with cardiac disease at high risk for ventricular dysrhythmias, ICDs are
effective in preventing ventricular dysrhythmias and sudden cardiac arrest [84, 107-109, 111-113].
However in the past the AHA/ACC guidelines have recommended against all moderate and high-
intensity sports for athletes with ICDs because the safety and efficacy of these devices during sport
competition was unknown. Recently, studies have reported that athletes primarily with HCM or long
QT syndrome with LV ejection fractions in the normal or the mildly reduced range may be able to
participate safely in noncontact or low contact competitive sports with a low risk of life-threatening
events [113-116]. In these studies appropriate, as well as inappropriate shocks due to T-wave over-
sensing, supraventricular or sinus tachycardia, and lead malfunction, have been reported. A limitation
of some of these studies is that ICD shocks have been self-reported by the athletes or their care givers
and these individuals may have purposefully withheld information about ICD shocks in order to
continue sports participation. Nevertheless, the AHA/ACC currently has Class II recommendations for
athletes with ICDs where participation in sports may be considered if the risk of adverse outcomes
appears to be low or disease-specific management may reduce the risk to acceptable levels [117,118].
 In addition, the European Association of Preventive Cardiology recommends that return to play
decisions be made after thorough discussion and shared decision making by the physician(s) with the
athlete with the ICD, the interested parties (care providers, coaches, institutions and/or organizations)
of the “four Ds”:   (1) the underlying cardiac disease; (2) the danger to the athlete, third parties
involved, and the environment; (3) the device; and (4) the risk of dysrhthymias or ICD shocks [119].

  When significant debate or doubt occurs regarding the participation of an athlete with an ICD in
competitive sports, consultation should be obtained from medical experts in sports medicine,
cardiomyopathies and ICDs. In athletes where a consensus decision is made that return to play is
desirable and permissible, maximal effort exercise testing should be performed to evaluate for
inducible dysrhythmias prior to sports participation and the treatment of the athlete adjusted if
necessary [120].

tachycardia programming, such as high-rate tachycardia cutoff (200 beats per minute) and long-

 "evidenceSummary":"Descriptive epidemiological analysis of official NFL gamebook records of in-game injuries in regular-season games from 2011 to 2015, covering 27,712 injuries across 1,280 games (80 Thursday, 85 Monday, 1,115 Sunday). Mean injuries per game were 21.7 on Thursdays, 21.4 on Sundays and 18.2 on Mondays. Thursday and Sunday did not differ (p = 0.9264), but Monday games had fewer injuries than Sunday (p = 0.0028) and Thursday (p = 0.0214), and a team's injuries did not differ between the weeks before and after its Thursday game.",
 "screeningLimitations":"This is a descriptive count from one league over five regular seasons, with only 80 Thursday games and no adjustment for player exposure or opponent. Injuries were recorded by league officials in gamebooks, so counts may be incomplete, and the design cannot show that the schedule causes injury differences.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the non-significant Thursday-Sunday difference as proof that short-week games carry no added injury risk, when the study had only 80 Thursday games and the authors say their small sample may explain why they found a slight increase where earlier studies found a decrease.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2023,
   "citation":"Sharma A, Fletcher AN, Shah JK, Akoh CC, Parekh SG. The Effect of Thursday Night Football on Injuries in the National Football League. Journal of Orthopedics and Sports Medicine. 2023;5(3):304-310.",
   "doi":"10.26502/josm.511500115",
   "abstract":"Analysed NFL gamebook records of in-game injuries in regular-season games from 2011 to 2015, comparing injury counts by weekday, season week and position. Thursday games had about the same number of injuries as Sunday games, Monday games had fewer, and a team's injuries did not change in the weeks before or after its Thursday game.",
   "tldr":"In NFL regular-season games from 2011 to 2015, Thursday games did not have significantly more in-game injuries than Sunday games, and Monday games had fewer. Injury counts rose later in the season.",
   "methods":"Descriptive epidemiological study of official NFL gamebook data for regular-season games from 2011 to 2015. Injury counts per game were compared by weekday, season quarter and position with one-way ANOVA and Tukey's HSD tests, and each team's injuries were compared across the Thursday game and the weeks before and after it.",
   "findings":"Mean in-game injuries per game were 21.4 on Sundays (1,115 games), 18.2 on Mondays (85 games) and 21.7 on Thursdays (80 games). Thursday versus Sunday gave p = 0.9264, and Monday had fewer injuries than Sunday (p = 0.0028) and Thursday (p = 0.0214). Injuries per team were 10.8 in the week before and 10.8 in the Thursday game, and 10.7 in the week after (p = 0.4971 and p = 0.7315). Week 17 had about twice the injury rate of Week 1 (31.1 vs 15.7 per game).",
   "limitations":"The authors note that their sample of 80 Thursday games gave limited power, and that gamebook reporting may be inconsistent. The text gives the 2011 total as 4,467 while Table 2 gives 4,496, and it gives mean injuries per game for 2014 as 23.5 (13.3) while Table 2 gives 18.8 (4.7). The analysis is limited to regular-season games and does not adjust for exposure or opponent.",
   "practicalImplications":"Staff planning short-week schedules should note that these data show no clear added injury count for Thursday games, but a small increase cannot be ruled out. The authors suggest education on tackling technique and strength and conditioning for defensive players, and they suggest alternating Thursday and Sunday games with Monday games.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: Staff can use these findings to think about how game spacing relates to in-game injury counts across a season, and to plan injury-prevention work for defensive positions. The study counted injuries only and did not measure performance, fatigue or recovery in individual players.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: The study does not address individual return-to-play decisions, re-injury after return, or the timing of return. The finding of no residual effect on the following week's injury count applies to team-level counts and cannot guide when an injured player should return."
 }
}

The Effect of Thursday Night Games
on In-Game Injury Rates in the
National Football League
Jose R. Perez,*† MD, Jonathan Burke,‡ MPH, Abdul K. Zalikha,‡ MD, Dhanur Damodar,† MD,
Joseph S. Geller,‡ BA, Andrew N.L. Buskard,† PhD, Lee D. Kaplan,† MD,
and Michael G. Baraga,† MD
Investigation performed at University of Miami Sports Medicine Institute,
University of Miami Miller School of Medicine, Miami, Florida, USA

Background: Although claims of increased injury rates with Thursday night National Football League (NFL) games exist, a paucity
of data exist substantiating these claims.
Purpose: To evaluate the effect of rest between games on in-game injury rates as it pertains to overall injury incidence, location,
and player position.
Study Design: Descriptive epidemiologic study.
Methods: Data were obtained from official NFL game books for regular season games from all 32 teams for the 2013-2016
seasons. All in-game injuries recorded in official game books were included. Rest periods between games were classified as
short (4 days), regular (6-8 days), or long (10 days). Overall observed injury rates per team-game were analyzed in relation to
different rest periods using negative binomial regression. For results with significant overall findings, pairwise comparisons were
tested using the Wald chi-square test. Exploratory secondary analyses were performed in a similar fashion to assess differences in
injury rates for the different rest periods when stratified by anatomic location and player position.
Results: A total of 2846 injuries were identified throughout the 4 seasons. There was an overall significant difference in injuries per
team-game between short, regular, and long rest (P ¼ .01). With short rest, an observed mean of 1.26 injuries per game (95% CI,
1.06-1.49) was significantly different from the 1.53 observed injuries per game with regular rest (95% CI, 1.46-1.60; P ¼ .03), but not
compared with the 1.34 observed injuries per game with long rest (P ¼ .56). For player position, only the tight end, linebacker, and
fullback group demonstrated significant differences between the injury rates for different rest categories. Quarterback was the only
position with more injuries during games played on Thursday compared with both regular and long rest. This specific analysis was
underpowered and the difference was not significant (P ¼ .08). No differences were found regarding injury rates in correlation with
differences in rest periods with different injury locations.
Conclusion: A short rest period between games is not associated with increased rates of observed injuries reported in NFL game
books; rather, our data suggest there are significantly fewer injuries for Thursday night games compared with games played on
regular rest. Future research correlating rest and quarterback injury rates is warranted.
Keywords: football (American); epidemiology; general sports trauma; injury prevention

compared with the 1.34 observed injuries per game with long rest (P ¼ .56). For player position, only the tight end, linebacker, and
fullback group demonstrated significant differences between the injury rates for different rest categories. Quarterback was the only
position with more injuries during games played on Thursday compared with both regular and long rest. This specific analysis was
underpowered and the difference was not significant (P ¼ .08). No differences were found regarding injury rates in correlation with
differences in rest periods with different injury locations.
Conclusion: A short rest period between games is not associated with increased rates of observed injuries reported in NFL game
books; rather, our data suggest there are significantly fewer injuries for Thursday night games compared with games played on
regular rest. Future research correlating rest and quarterback injury rates is warranted.
